zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The supplied subset aided entry identification and coverage; this review’s readings and English notes are independent and remain controlled by the supplied BnF scan.

lines.note: Mozu is a bird compared with a shrike. Mo- begins mozu no kusaguki, the example naming the prey impaled by the bird; it also confirms the preceding page's catchword.
Zuno completes mozu no, followed by kusaguki. P. is a separate usage label; the Portuguese identifies small creatures or frogs, rather than another Japanese synonym.

runs.text: que eſte paßaro deixa eſpetadas nos bambus, ou

lines.note: The bird leaves these creatures impaled on bamboo or sticks. Preserve the printed feminine eſpetadas after the mixed list rather than grammatically regularizing the source.

runs.text: paos pera quando não tem que comer que he no

lines.note: The impaled prey is explained as food kept for a time when the bird has nothing to eat. The clause ends with the season on the next row.

Inuerno completes the account of winter food. The separate far-right ( dia. is displaced text completing eſcorregadia in the following entry; it is retained at its physical position, not joined to inuerno.

runs.text: Certa erua do mar muito eſcorrega

lines.note: Mozzucu is a very slippery sea plant. Eſcorrega continues in the displaced dia. above; no terminal hyphen is securely printed on this row.

Mozzucubiyaxiru names a cold broth made with the sea plant. Xiru is embedded Japanese inside the Portuguese explanation. The upright-looking capital X and italic lowercase iru retain the draft's mixed type treatment rather than forcing a whole-word font.

runs.text: que ſe faz com esta erua.

lines.note: The broth is made with this plant, completing the mozzuku entry. The following internal heading begins a new alphabetical subsection.
Mu is explained by nashi, absence or nonexistence. The scan contains the enlarged two-line initial M before the small capital V; the draft lost M and treated the row as indented.
Zaru completes mu de gozaru: being nothing or not existing. The row is indented beneath the enlarged initial and remains separate physical text.

Muaku fuzoo is defined as committing every kind of sin. The negative elements in the Japanese phrase do not justify reversing the source's explicit Portuguese meaning; final S. is a written-language label.
Mubai, paraphrased nakadachi nashi, means having no intermediary. The Portuguese gives the same third-person or mediator sense.
No one is available to intercede, completing the mediator definition. The final S. label is upright rather than italic prose.
Mube is equated with genimo, truly or with good reason. The intervening label is P., not the draft F.; its print is upright.
Verdade completes em verdade, the second paraphrase of mube. This short continuation belongs to that entry, not to the next health-related headword.
Mubyoo is explained by yamai nashi, absence of illness. Boa diſpoſição accordingly refers to being in good health.

runs.text: Peßoa bem deſposta, ou que não he

lines.note: Mubyoona describes a healthy person. Preserve the historical deſposta in the Portuguese, without inserting the modern vowel of disposta.
Doente completes the negative phrase: someone who is not sick. It is a continuation of mubyoona, not a separate definition.
Mubyoosha is a person free of illness. Idem points back to the healthy person just described.
Mubut sekaina mono describes a person lacking refinement and religious concern. The Portuguese starts with absence of primor, not a literal account of an empty world.

runs.text: nem corteſia, & que não tem deuer com a

lines.note: The description adds lack of courtesy and lack of concern for what follows. The printed phrase ter deuer com is retained as part of the source's wording.
Saluação completes the religious concern missing from the person described. This is the last part of a three-row definition.
Mukaba means the front teeth. The clear Portuguese Dentes corrects the draft Denites, which inserted a nonexistent i.

runs.text: Certo calçado de couro que ſerue

lines.note: Mukabaki is described as a kind of leather footwear or leg covering. The next row specifies the occasions on which it is used.

runs.text: na caça, ou em outros certos folguedos.

lines.note: The leather covering is used in hunting and certain entertainments. These uses qualify mukabaki rather than introducing new entries.
Mukade is a centipede. Centopeya is the historical Portuguese spelling in the scan and is not modernized.
Mukai is glossed as opposite or facing. This short positional entry is distinct from the conjugated verb below.
Mukai, with its principal parts, means turning toward somewhere or placing oneself opposite. The printed long-o forms retain their downward marks.
The positional gloss ends in de fronte. Haru ni mukoo then illustrates approaching spring; Chegar continues with the reflexive particle below.
Se a primauera completes the approach to spring. Teki ni mukoo is the contrasting example of going out to face an enemy.
Ao encontro ao imigo completes the enemy-facing example. Preserve imigo rather than expanding it to modern inimigo.
The noun mukai means going to meet someone. Mukai ni sanzuru begins a series of alternative verbs for going out to meet.
Mairu and izzuru continue the alternative verbs meaning to go out to meet. Mu- begins a new example of sending someone to meet another person.
Kaini completes mukaini; tsukawasu and yaru are alternatives for sending. Mandar ao en- starts the matching Portuguese phrase.
Contro completes encontro, finishing the sending-to-meet example. The row is a short continuation, not a displaced catchword.
Mukaibune is a vessel sent or going out to meet someone. The Portuguese definition is complete on this row.
Mukai tsubute is illustrated with the verb suru, referring to throwing stones at one another. The next rows explain a preferred expression.

runs.text: Iugar às pedradas: mas a propria palaura be

lines.note: The gloss describes stone-throwing play and introduces the proper expression below. The final be-like form is retained: its lower bowl appears closed, unlike the clear h in c1-l004. Portuguese he is expected, so this remains a nonblocking glyph caveat.
Ingi wo suru is the alternative expression supplied inside the Portuguese sentence about the proper term. The scan prints this Japanese phrase in italic type; it is not an independent headword.
Mukaitori is referred to the preferred mukayetoru form by Meliùs. The editorial Latin is italic, while the Japanese cross-reference is upright.
The action is going out to receive someone. Koe wo tazunete begins a quotation about seeking the voices of those who call, with taz- divided before zunete.
Zunete completes tazunete, followed by the honorific prospective form of receiving or welcoming. The quotation's gui continues as gui gia across the row boundary.
The quotation urges care not to neglect nenbutsu. Vocota- is the start of the negative admonition completed below, not a new lexical item.
Raxerarena completes the warning not to neglect the invocation. Feiq. is the upright source label, followed by italic Lib. 2. and the beginning of the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Fotoque vindo em buſca, & ao encontro dos

lines.note: The Portuguese names Fotoque as the one who comes seeking and meeting those who call. Fotoque is an embedded Japanese term; the relative clause continues in the next column.

runs.text: que o chamão os leua pera ſi, olhai que não

lines.note: Continues the translation from column 1: those who call are taken to him, followed by a warning. The opening que is running text, not a new entry or a duplicated line.

runs.text: falteis, ou vos deſcuideis em o inuocar.

lines.note: The warning is not to fail or become careless in invoking him. This closes the quoted example under mukaitori.
Mukaiuma is a horse going out to meet someone. The medial v in Mucaivma retains the source's positional spelling for the vowel of uma.
Mukaizura is a frontage or something facing one. The definition continues with de fronte on the next row.
De fronte completes the facing-position gloss. The final upright B. is a usage label, not part of the italic explanation.

runs.text: Dia que reſponde de pois do anno

lines.note: Mukawaribi is the corresponding day after a year, an anniversary. Preserve the printed separation de pois rather than silently making depois.

runs.text: ao dia em que hum morreo, ou fez algũa cou-

lines.note: The anniversary refers to the day someone died or performed a notable deed. Cou- continues as couſa below.
Sa notauel completes the reference to a notable act. This closes the anniversary-day entry.
Mukawarizuki is the corresponding month in the following year. Its definition parallels the preceding anniversary-day term.

runs.text: reſpõde a outro em q̃ hũ morreo, a doeceo, &c.

lines.note: The month corresponds to a death, illness, or similar event. The printed a doeceo spacing is retained; semantically it is the verb for becoming ill.
Mukashi means formerly or in olden times. Mukashi wo shinobu begins an example of longing for the past, divided after xi-.
Nobu completes shinobu. The Portuguese saudades describes nostalgic longing for things past.
Antiguas completes the paired description of past and old things. The historical spelling retains its u.
Mukashigatari is talk or narration about past events. Pratica here refers to discourse, not to practical exercise.
Antiguas completes the description of bygone matters. This continuation closes mukashigatari before the adjectival form below.
Mukashi no is an attributive expression for something old or former. The printed Mucaxino remains a single string.
Mukaye means inviting or calling someone to one's house. The object and destination are completed in the next row.
Kyaku wo mukayuru illustrates inviting or receiving a guest. Item then introduces a second, marital application of the verb.

runs.text: Caſar o homem com molher, ou chamàla a

lines.note: The second application is a man marrying a woman or calling her to his house. Preserve molher and chamàla as the historical printed forms.
Tsuma wo mukayuru illustrates taking a wife into one's household. Sua caſa completes the Portuguese sentence begun on the preceding row.
Mukayetori directs the reader to mukaitori, where the detailed gloss and quotation appear. Vide is italic Latin; the referenced headword is upright.
Muchi is explained by chie nashi, lack of knowledge or wisdom. Ignorancia is the complete Portuguese equivalent here.
A separate muchi means a riding switch or whip. Muchi ni abumi wo awa- begins an expression combining whip and stirrup.

runs.text: Ir a todo correr, ou com

lines.note: Suru completes awasuru; soyuru is the alternative verb. The whole expression means going at full speed or with great haste.
Muchi wo susumuru supplies another expression for urging the horse on. Grande preſſa closes the preceding haste gloss.
The example begins with an urgent journey and a horse being led. Fiqi vma- retains the source's separation and initial v rather than modernizing the compound.

runs.text: ni muchiuo ſuſumete xeqi yamauo vchi-

lines.note: The traveller urges the horse with the whip and crosses the mountain barrier. Vchi- begins the prefixed crossing verb continued below.
Koyenu completes uchikoyenu, a completed crossing in this narrative, not a modern negative. The Portuguese begins by describing travel in great haste.

runs.text: daua no caualo que leuaua pello cabreſto com

lines.note: The traveller strikes the horse being led by its halter. The source's cabreſto and pello are retained in the literal explanation.

runs.text: a vara, & paſſaua pellos montes, & ſerras.

lines.note: The switch is used while passing through mountains and ranges. This completes the translation of the preceding Japanese journey example.

runs.text: Vara com que dão no ca-

lines.note: Misemuchi names the whip use explained as striking a horse on the right side of the neck. Ca- begins caualo below.

runs.text: ualo na parte direita do peſcoço. ¶

lines.note: Ualo completes caualo and the right-side description. Cacu- introduces the contrasting kakushi-muchi term on the same row.

runs.text: Vara com que ſe da no peſcoço

lines.note: Xi muchi completes kakushi muchi. The Portuguese begins the corresponding description of striking the horse's neck on the other side.
The side is the left: da parte eſquerda. The scan reads da, correcting draft do before parte.
Muchuu is glossed by yume no uchi, in a dream. The scan prints vchi with positional v, not the draft uchi; Mu- begins the following example.
Muchuu no tei de gozaru describes the condition of being in a dream. The Portuguese begins an explanation of someone's state while sleeping.
Sleeping and dreaming complete the explanation of muchuu no tei. This is not a new headword for sleep.
Mukoo, alternatively bukoo, is paraphrased koo nashi, lack of accomplishment or experience. The scan reads l, bucô, not a word Ibucǒ; the three visible long-o marks are circumflexes.

runs.text: cia. ¶ Item, Não ter proueito nem pre-

lines.note: Cia completes experiencia. A further sense is receiving neither benefit nor reward, with pre- beginning premio below.
Mio completes premio: no reward from work or service. The final upright S. marks the written-language usage.
Muko means son-in-law. Muko wo toru and muko-dori wo suru illustrate taking a son-in-law; the final mark after muco is a visible hyphen, not the draft period.

runs.text: Caſar a filha, ou tomar genro.

lines.note: Dori wo suru completes the compound example. The Portuguese gives marrying off one's daughter or taking a son-in-law.
Mukoiri wo suru describes the son-in-law entering the household. The following row specifies whose house and the purpose.

runs.text: do ſogro pera caſar com a filha.

lines.note: The house is the father-in-law's, entered to marry his daughter. This completes the example of mukoiri.
Mukookaze is a contrary wind or wind from ahead. Por proa supplies the nautical description of a headwind.

Mukodori and mukoiri direct the reader back to Muco, the son-in-law entry above. The small c in the cross-reference is abraded but its faint trace and the explicit reference support Muco over draft Muo.
Mukonbon is glossed as without beginning. Bup. marks Buddhist terminology and remains upright before the italic explanation.
